Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.

- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
I have always loved the hour just before the library closes for the night. The light turns amber, dust hangs in the air, and every book seems to breathe a little slower. It is not silence, exactly, because silence would be empty, and this is full. It is the sound of pages remembering hands, of chairs remembering weight, of rain remembering roofs it has not yet touched. I walk between the shelves without looking for anything in particular, which is the best way to find something true. A spine cracks, a margin sighs, and suddenly I am ten years old.

When I was ten, I believed libraries were ships that had learned how to sit still. Each aisle was a deck, each window a porthole, each librarian a patient captain watching weather inside other people. I would press my ear to the atlases and listen for oceans that existed only on paper. Some maps showed countries that no longer existed, and that felt honest to me even then. Places disappear, people rename them, borders move like tired rivers, but ink holds its breath a little longer. I learned early that loss is not always loud or sudden. Sometimes it whispers.

As an adult I still walk as if I am shelving thoughts back where they belong. Morning is for lists, for bread, for keys, for the small negotiations we make with gravity and time. Evening is for wandering, for letting the city unbutton its bright and hurried coat. Streetlights come on one by one, not all at once, as if someone is remembering them individually. Shopkeepers sweep thresholds that nobody will cross until tomorrow, yet they sweep with ceremonial care. There is dignity in maintaining a doorway for strangers who have not arrived yet. I try to remember that daily.

My grandmother measured nothing, yet everything she cooked tasted like an argument won by love. She would taste soup and declare it needed more patience, which was her word for salt and waiting. Her kitchen windows fogged even in summer, as if the room were dreaming out loud. I stood on a stool beside her, learning that recipes are stories we agree to repeat with our hands. Some stories improve when you change them, some break, and some wait years for the right tongue. When she died, we found notebooks filled with quantities like handful, enough, until it sings. Enough.

I think every person should stand alone before the sea at least once without taking a photograph. The sea does not pose, does not explain, does not care whether you understand its grammar of returning. It gives back bottles, shoes, ropes, and sometimes the exact sentence you threw away years ago. Standing there, you learn scale without humiliation, because vastness can be a kindness. Your grief is not diminished, only placed beside something older that knows how to carry it. Waves do not solve sorrow, they rehearse endurance until the body believes endurance is possible. That is no small gift.

Language is the only suitcase that gets heavier the more generously you share what is inside. A word given away does not leave you poorer, it leaves you practiced in abundance. I love untranslatable words because they prove that feeling has local weather. Some languages have a word for the light through leaves, others for missing someone before they leave. We borrow these words like umbrellas, grateful, a little damp, and changed by the borrowing. To speak carefully is not to speak fearfully, it is to remember that sentences build rooms others must live in. Choose the windows with mercy.

I worry that we are training ourselves to skim the surface of everything, including our own lives. We scroll past funerals and festivals with the same thumb, and the thumb learns a terrible neutrality. Attention is not merely time spent, it is the direction in which love learns to look. That is why reading slowly feels radical now, almost monastic, a refusal to be hurried out of wonder. A paragraph can be a garden if you enter it without demanding fruit immediately. Some meanings ripen only after you have closed the book and washed the dishes and slept. Wait patiently.

I keep a private archive of strangers who were kind to me for no discoverable reason. The bus driver who waited while I ran, wet newspaper clutched like a failing flag. The woman in Lisbon who drew me a map on a napkin and then drew a star where pastries lived. The old man who taught me to whistle using a blade of grass and unlimited confidence. None of them know they live in my memory rent free, luminous, unconsulted. Perhaps someone archives me that way too, for a door held, a sentence softened, a shared umbrella. I hope so.

Hope, I have decided, is not optimism wearing a brighter coat, it is work done in the dark. Optimism says things will improve, hope rolls up its sleeves before any evidence arrives. It plants trees whose shade it may never sit in, and calls that planting a form of prayer. It teaches children songs in languages that empires tried to erase from the throat. It saves seeds, mends coats, writes letters, learns names, and refuses to confuse despair with sophistication. Cynicism is easy because it never has to build anything that disappointment could knock down. Hope risks being beautifully wrong.

Tonight the librarian will tap the desk gently and say we have fifteen minutes left. People will surface from their chapters like swimmers, blinking, reluctant, carrying other centuries in their arms. I will choose one book, not the best book, just the book that chose me back. Outside, the city will be doing its neon arithmetic, counting taxis, windows, and unfinished promises. I will walk home slowly, practicing attention, carrying soup, maps, seas, grandmothers, and strangers inside me. And if life is a library, then kindness is leaving useful notes in the margins for whoever opens us next. Begin again.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: MID

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW. A lyrical first-person meditation uses recurring images and intimate memories to give its reflections a distinct emotional texture.

## Grounded reading
The voice is tender, observant, and deliberately unhurried, finding feeling in the hour before a library closes, a grandmother’s soup, a swept doorway, and kindness from strangers. Its pathos comes from treating loss as quiet and ongoing: vanished places, a dead grandmother, and grief beside the sea are not solved, but held within larger practices of attention and endurance. The reader is invited to slow down, notice what would otherwise pass by, and leave some kindness for whoever comes next.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample returns to libraries, books, maps, language, and acts of care as ways of carrying memory. It foregrounds attention over speed, patient maintenance over spectacle, and hope as practical work rather than confidence that things will improve. The closing image of useful notes left in the margins gathers these themes into an ethic of kindness.

## Evidence line
> Attention is not merely time spent, it is the direction in which love learns to look.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the recurring imagery and consistent moral emphasis make this a distinctive, coherent expression of attentive tenderness.
